meta.title: Who really said "Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it is Shakespeare — Friar Laurence, at the close of Act 2, scene 3 of Romeo and Juliet. But he says "slow", not "slowly".
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Shakespeare: Friar Laurence's last line in Act 2, scene 3 of Romeo and Juliet, printed in the 1599 second quarto.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: It is the last line of Act 2, scene 3 of Romeo and Juliet — Friar Laurence’s parting shot as Romeo hurries off to arrange his same-day wedding. The line stands in the authoritative 1599 second quarto and in every modern edition descended from it, so the wording is confirmed.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
Act 2, scene 3 — the closing two lines
Quarto 2, 1599 — this passage is not in the 1597 first quarto (the play itself was first printed 1597)

source.excerpt:
ROMEO  O let us hence; I stand on sudden haste.
FRIAR LAURENCE  Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
trail: The Folger Shakespeare edition of Act 2, scene 3 ↗ ends the scene with Romeo’s “O, let us hence. I stand on sudden haste.” and the Friar’s reply, “Wisely and slow. They stumble that run fast.”
The Internet Shakespeare Editions’ modernised text of the 1599 second quarto ↗ carries the same exchange, giving the line as “Wisely and slow, they stumble that run fast.”

Wikipedia’s account of the play’s textual history ↗ records the 1597 first quarto as a probable memorial reconstruction and the 1599 second quarto — “Newly corrected, augmented and amended,” about 800 lines longer — as the text all later quartos, folios and modern editions derive from.
The free Project Gutenberg text of the play ↗ prints the same two lines with the semicolon that most circulating versions use, and Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Friar Laurence at Act II, scene iii.
source.excerptNote: Punctuation varies by editor and the words do not: the Folger text prints periods (“Wisely and slow. They stumble that run fast.”), the Internet Shakespeare Editions’ modernised second quarto a comma, and the Project Gutenberg text the semicolon shown here.

source.rightsNote: Romeo and Juliet was first printed in 1597 and its authoritative second quarto issued in 1599 by Thomas Creede for Cuthbert Burby ↗, so the text is far past any copyright term in the United States. Individual modern editions carry their own editorial apparatus, but these words are Shakespeare’s and free to quote.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet sometime between 1591 and 1595; it reached print in 1597 and again, in a far better text, in 1599. He is also the internet’s single largest magnet for invented quotations — which makes the genuine ones worth pinning down precisely. This is one of the genuine ones: eight words handed to a friar who is about to ignore his own advice.

misattribution.heading: Where it goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Shakespeare. What gets mangled is the wording, and who in the play actually says it.

items.why: The –ly form is everywhere, but no early text supports it. A podcast episode built entirely on the line titles it “Wisely and slowly, they stumble that run fast” ↗, credited to Shakespeare with no play named in the title. The quarto reads slow.

Goodreads files “Wisely and slowly; they stumble that run fast” as a quote by Hugh Howey, from Wool Omnibus ↗ — a 21st-century science-fiction novel. The words are Shakespeare’s, roughly four centuries earlier.

items.who: “Go wisely, and go slowly. Those who rush into things stumble.”
items.why: That is a study-guide translation, not Shakespeare — it is how LitCharts renders the line into current English ↗ alongside the original. Versions of this plain-English form circulate as if they were the quotation itself.
Quote sites strip the drama out of it. BrainyQuote gives it as “Wisely, and slow. They stumble that run fast.” with no play, scene or speaker ↗ — presenting a character’s line as the author’s maxim.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Friar Laurence’s, the last line of Act 2, scene 3 of Romeo and Juliet; the modernised text of the 1599 second quarto reads “Wisely and slow, they stumble that run fast” ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Romeo has known Juliet for a matter of hours. He turns up at Friar Laurence’s cell asking to be married that same day — to a Capulet — having spent the previous scenes in mourning over a different girl. The Friar notices: “Young men’s love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.”

He agrees anyway, and for a political reason rather than a romantic one: the match “may so happy prove / To turn your households’ rancor to pure love.” Then he sends Romeo off with a warning about speed — a warning the Friar is himself the first to ignore. The line reads as plain good sense in isolation, which is why it travels so well; in the play it is dramatic irony with a fuse on it.
detailsBody: Romeo and Juliet was first printed in 1597, in a quarto long regarded as a memorial reconstruction — a text apparently pieced together from the imperfect recollections of one or two actors. The 1599 second quarto advertises itself on its title page as “Newly corrected, augmented, and amended,” runs about 800 lines longer, and is thought to derive from Shakespeare’s own draft. All later quartos, the Folio and every modern edition descend from Q2 ↗, which is where this line comes to us from.
